_comment: The news of Rome (decided 2026-09-28): what history had happening in and around Rome, AD 155-175, heard as talk in the Forum. Text only: it changes nothing in the simulation, and the player meets these people only indirectly. The plague and the bust are not here: the simulation reports them. month is 1-12. Dates are the best-attested ones; where scholars differ, the text keeps to what is agreed.

news.text: Antoninus Pius has ruled for seventeen years and hasn't left Italy in all that time. People call it the quietest reign anyone can remember.
Marcus Aurelius, the emperor's adopted son and heir, shares his father's work. People say he'd rather read philosophy than watch the games.
Herodes Atticus, the richest man in Greece, is accused in Rome over the death of his wife Regilla. He is acquitted.

Antoninus Pius is dead at his villa at Lorium. His last watchword to the guard was 'equanimity'. Marcus Aurelius takes his place and makes his adoptive brother Lucius Verus co-emperor: two emperors at once, for the first time.
The new emperors find the treasury full: Antoninus left 2,700 million sesterces, and the money changers say it shows in the coin.
The empress Faustina gives birth to twin boys, Commodus and Antoninus.
The Tiber floods: houses collapse, grain stores are spoiled, and bread is dear. The emperors see to the relief themselves.
Bad news from the East: the Parthian king has seized Armenia and destroyed a Roman legion at Elegeia.
Lucius Verus leaves Rome to take command against Parthia.
A physician from Pergamum named Galen has arrived. He cuts open animals in public to show how the body works, and has already quarrelled with half the Physicians' Circle.
Statius Priscus takes Artaxata, the capital of Armenia.
Lucius Verus marries Lucilla, Marcus's daughter, at Ephesus.
Avidius Cassius's army has sacked Seleucia and burned the palace at Ctesiphon. Soldiers say something was let loose when they looted a temple at Seleucia.
Galen has left Rome for Pergamum, suddenly. His rivals say he ran from the sickness.
Marcus and Lucius celebrate their triumph over Parthia. The crowds are thinner than anyone expected.
Tribes from beyond the Danube have crossed into Pannonia. They were driven back, but the frontier is uneasy.
Both emperors leave for Aquileia and the northern frontier.
Lucius Verus is dead, struck down on the road home at Altinum. Marcus rules alone.
Galen is back in Rome at the emperor's command, to look after young Commodus.
Rather than raise taxes for the war, Marcus auctions the palace's treasures in Trajan's Forum: gold cups, crystal, silk robes, his wife's jewels. The sale runs for two months.
The Marcomanni and Quadi have broken through the Alps: Opitergium is burned and Aquileia besieged. It's the first enemy army in Italy in centuries.
Herdsmen of the Nile delta rise in revolt. Grain merchants at Ostia watch for the Alexandrian fleet, and Avidius Cassius is sent to put it down.
Marcus is still on the Danube, and has been for six years. Rome runs on letters from the front.

_localComment: Local news (decided 2026-09-28): invented street-level talk, one item every news.localEveryMonths. Items tied to the player's world (when) come first; the rest follow in order; each is heard once. when: always (default), fountain, workshop, member:<institution id>, plague:warning, plague:outbreak, plague:passed, bust:warning, prices:<percent up since AD 155>. from / until: years. month (1-12): a festival, heard on the turn that covers that month, whatever the cadence. {leader:<id>} is that institution's leader now. Text only: changes nothing.

local.text: People on your street say the stranger who fixed the district fountain must be an engineer from Alexandria. The women queuing there before dawn have stopped boiling the water.
The smith at the forges tells anyone who'll listen about his odd new partner, who draws machines on wax tablets and never says where he learned it.
{leader:guild} complains at the baths that the grain ships from Alexandria are late again, and that the guild's warehouses at Ostia are half empty.
The guild's feast for its patron god runs late into the night. {leader:guild} makes a long speech about honest weights; half the room is laughing.
{leader:faction} has a new client at his morning greeting: a young lawyer from Africa who talks too fast. The faction's regulars are wary.
{leader:faction} is pushing a young client for the praetorship. The Senate chooses, but a crowd cheering outside the Curia doesn't hurt, and the faction is paying for the wine.
{leader:circle} tells her students she knew Galen's father, an architect in Pergamum, and that the son was always this insufferable.
The healers of the Tiber Island sanctuary have a new crop of thank-offerings: clay feet, eyes and ears, left by people who got better.
{leader:bank} has moved his counting tables closer to the Temple of Castor. Depositors say it makes them feel safer; he says it's the light.
{leader:junian} gives a dinner for three hundred. The Caecilians did not come.
A fuller's family on the next street is down with a fever. The neighbours keep their children indoors and leave bread at the door.
Amulet sellers in the Subura have sold out of everything with a picture of Apollo on it. The price of a sprig of rue has tripled.
Carts go through the Subura at dawn now. Nobody on your street talks about what's in them.
The baker who shouted every morning on the corner is gone; his wife bakes alone and says nothing. The queue is shorter than it was.
Workshops are hiring again, and paying more than before the sickness: there are fewer hands to go round.
The moneychangers on the Via Sacra weigh every coin twice now. One shows you a denarius that's more copper than silver.
Your landlord raises the rent again and blames the price of bread. The baker blames the price of wheat. Nobody blames the mint out loud.
Shopkeepers are buying up stock with borrowed money; everyone says prices can only go up.
A five-storey tenement near the Circus Flaminius collapses in the night. The landlord says it was the rain; the tenants say it was the landlord.
Fire in the Subura: the night watch passes buckets along the street for hours and pulls down two houses to stop it.
The aediles seize a baker's loaves on the Vicus Tuscus: his loaves were a quarter short of the weight he sold them at.
The Greens win four races in a row at the Circus Maximus. A Blue supporter is found tied to a statue the next morning, unharmed but furious.
A retiarius nobody had heard of beats the crowd's favourite at the games; the betting shops are paying out for days.
Someone at the Baths of Trajan has scratched a curse on a lead tablet: 'To whoever stole my tunic: may you lose your sleep and your eyes.'
The grain dole is handed out at the Porticus Minucia; the line stretches past the Theatre of Balbus.
The price of Spanish olive oil jumps after a ship goes down off Sardinia. The oil sellers of the Velabrum say they'll recover; the cooks don't believe them.
A new bathhouse opens on the Esquiline with heated floors and a painted ceiling of sea creatures. Entry is a quadrans; the queue goes round the block.
Two neighbours on the Aventine have been in court for a year over a shared wall. The wall has now fallen down on its own.
A sailor at Ostia swears he saw an elephant loaded onto a grain ship bound for Rome. Nobody believes him until it's walked up the Via Ostiensis.
The Saturnalia: masters serve at table, everyone wears the felt cap, and your neighbour gives you a candle and a very small cheese.
The Compitalia: every crossroads shrine in the city is hung with wool dolls, and the street associations feast until late.
The Floralia: the games run for days, the theatre is rowdier than usual, and someone lets hares and goats loose in the Circus.
The Ludi Romani open with a procession from the Capitol to the Circus Maximus. The whole street empties to watch.
The Tiber rises to the steps of the Emporium and stops there. The warehousemen move everything to the upper floors anyway.
A seller of garum from Pompeii swears his fish sauce is the best in Italy. He's been saying it for thirty years; his competitors say it's the same barrel.
A philosopher in a filthy cloak lectures outside the Library of Trajan on how possessions are a burden. He asks for coins afterward.
The vigiles arrest a gang who'd been renting out the same room in a tenement to four families at once.
A wedding procession comes down your street: torches, flute players, walnuts thrown to the children, and a lot of very crude songs.
A burial club on the Via Appia holds its monthly dinner. Members pay a little each month so that none of them is thrown in a common pit.
A letter-writer at the Forum reads and writes for those who can't: two asses a letter, more for love letters.
A new book-seller opens by the Argiletum. The latest poems are copied while you wait; the scribes are fast and not always accurate.
The wine merchants say this year's Falernian is the best in a decade. They said the same last year.
A dog found asleep on the steps of the Temple of Saturn every morning is now being fed by half the Forum. Someone has named it Quaestor.
A mime show at the Theatre of Marcellus mocks a magistrate so openly that he walks out. The audience cheers louder.
A glassblower near the Porta Capena is selling cups so thin you can see your fingers through them. The rich are buying them by the dozen.
The aqueduct at the Porta Maggiore is closed for repairs; the fountains on the Esquiline run slow for a month.
A soothsayer in the Forum Boarium predicts the end of the world for the third time this year. His business is doing fine.
Brick stamps tell you who owns the kilns: half the new bricks in Rome carry the marks of a few senatorial families.
A man sues a barber whose razor slipped while a ball hit his hand from the street game next door. The lawyers argue over who's to blame.
A rich freedman's funeral goes down the Sacred Way with hired mourners, a mime wearing the dead man's mask, and a band.
